lines: When you artificially create barriers based on your preference for your brand authenticity, you prevent collaboration and collaboration is the lifeblood of this art form.
Instead, it's a throwback to the shit talk and stick up kid anthems of the duo’s Reagan era youth.
It's a blistering 33 minute doomsday shit talk and kick-your-fucking-head-in anthems--perfect for your next vacation to the scenic shores of Apokolips.

lines: With posthumous albums, it can be hard to tell where they fall between earnest creative tribute and cash grab.
His music was inspired by the swerving 808s and super-charged snares of UK drill, itself a refraction of Chicago’s original, but what you heard most was that voice.
It’s the track immediately after, “Something Special,” that really does the best job of intertwining his romantic side with his street sensibilities.

lines: It may not surface upon first listen, but the most rewarding works are those that require, well, work.
Any loop digger with an MPC can claim to be an archaeologist, but only the maddest mystic can resurrect the dusty, fragmented vinyl shards.
Danny Brown rolls up with his midwestern brethren on smoker’s anthem “High,” tracing his predilection for the purple back to his not-so-distant days on the block.

lines: Throughout his career, he’s prided himself on reinvention and versatility, while still being able to make whatever rap style he chooses his own.
The Youtube short is a beautifully-animated, self-referential acid trip, a product of two minds raised on Adult Swim.
“‘Cosmic.m4a’” sounds like it could have been heard during a fight in Cowboy Bebop, while “Lay_Up.m4a” features eerie instrumentals you’d expect to hear in a demented haunted house.

lines: But that’s not to suggest that the album is soulless, corporate drivel.
Even Diddy, who is rarely believable as anything beyond ruthless capitalist, acquits himself nicely with a song-ending monologue about disappointing his family.

“Ambitionz” is a naked Tupac lift, while “Bad For You” and “All Eyes On You” are cheeseball thug-in-love songs that seems contractually obligated to exist on every mainstream gangster rap album for the last 10 years.

lines: This album release, as well as the hype surrounding it, has proved to be nothing less than a profound (if not confused) cultural statement.
A thermometer in the maw of media and social relations, telling us more about what we like, desire, and value than any academic or author could ever hope to.
It’s no secret that before 808’s, such a technique was considered philistine-- strictly for those artists who couldn’t cut their teeth with the more key-savvy singers and producers.

lines: It’s transactional: the man will shatter your nervous system with the bars, so give your props accordingly.
He’s telling you to give him the flowers while he can still smell them, and it’s not a question or a request.
“Can’t be sniffin’ ye if you got a pimp to pay, if I’m insensitive just say,” the New York emcee says on “Choosin Fees.” No punches are held.

lines: A year removed from early 2020’s shorter, more straightforward Time Served, this album does contain newer forms of experimentation.
The lead single is “Time Today,” a track with a hook so subtly infectious it reappears often in everyday scenarios.
On “Shottas (La La),” he repeats the song’s title in a stop-and-start, stuttery way for the hook, then raps descriptive braggadocious one-liners in a smooth cadence in between.

lines: In an era where much of rap is taking poolside selfies as the world burns, they present hip hop as musical shadow work, dread incantations from the collective unconscious that bounce in appealingly eccentric ways.
But to hear it is to traverse an organic dreamscape where neither dark mood nor epiphany lingers too long, less a series of songs than a series of fugues.

The result is an album that lands squarely between the steely paranoia of their 2018 masterpiece Paraffin and the looser, more buoyant Shrines, a twilight forest of ideas that’s worth getting lost in.
puzzles.hed: "Ain't No Saving Us, Ain’t No Slaving Us:" Armand Hammer and The Alchemist's 'Haram'

lines: It’s too long, not thematically consistent, and has too many songs that sound the same.
Something like a more relatable and lighter 21 Savage, a more restrained Thug, a more accessible Future.
My Turn, bolstered by the same-year release of a (Deluxe Edition), was the most-streamed album of 2020.

lines: The tracks are messy and incomplete, half-finished sketches bloated with big ideas but lacking in basic song structure.
By employing all these thinly-sketched characters, he obscures the most powerful parts of his best work--his own thoughts, his own voice.
“How Much A Dollar Cost” and “Mortal Man” are corny concept tracks, the latter featuring a naked brand integration seance of 2Pac's ghost.

lines: All of which makes it hard to rate this album as a whole; the tracks that work are fantastic, while the missteps are truly abhorrent.
Worse, for a guy who prides himself on being cool, it’s undeniably corny: there is nothing less cool than collaborating with this generation’s answer to Vanilla Ice or Fred Durst.
"1-Train’s" epic posse cut is blog-bait but it’s loveable blog bait that unites all of your favorite rappers for the world’s best BET cypher.

lines: His humor is freshly refined -- it’s still absurdist but more self-deprecating instead of at the expense of someone else, and that’s a good thing.
He credited Westside Gunn, curator extraordinaire, for making him want to rap again.
His debut Bastard introduced the world to a teenage wunderkind with an insane amount of raw potential.

lines: Ultimately, he beat back his issues, killed his own Darkseid, and returned to the studio to deliver his most confident album to date.
He takes the point of view that if he did want to die, he should be able to explain exactly what his life was and what he’d leave behind.

On past records, he named songs after his heroes (“Silkk da Shocka” and “Tity and Dolla” on Tirade, “RIP Kevin Miller” and “Webbie Flow (U Like)” on Cilvia)—and he does so here once, naming “Chad” after Pimp C.

He also uses the pandemic as a loose thematic anchoring the way DOOM did with grub on MM..
Lines about the “singular current event” aren’t as commonplace as Omicron, but do pop up with unavoidable regularity like they do nowadays in regular conversation regardless.

lines: He writes songs from an insular, near-sociopathic, point-of-view unconcerned with the perspective of seemingly anyone besides himself.
Taking a cue from the viral success of recent releases from Beyoncé, D'Angelo and J.Cole, the mixtape almost instantaneously reached 500,000 in digital sales—without any prominent single.
Songs like "Legend," "Company" and "Energy" are overtly formulaic and filled with hashtag-ready lyrics for sycophantic retweeting.

lines: An exaltation of optimism amidst fear that seeks to do nothing more than do just that – exalt.
A composition that proclaims “That’s love/I love you” over and over and over again as an interlude.
The key phrase is “for the fun of it.” There’s a reason Action Bronson sounds so amused on the back of the same song.

lines: Instead of processing fame as a cross to bear as "Rap Star Slash Martyr," he sounds ready to shirk the whole thing at any minute.
Now, he’s railing against his label, Sony, for botching the roll out of a thirty-minute album that’s reportedly been finished for months.
On “AM / Radio,” he follows the tremendous turn from Ratking’s Wiki by snapping upright, darting through a fractured timeline littered with numerals and slurs.

lines: He carefully breaks syllables apart, masking his virtuosic flexibility with a mean mug.
They range from hyper-detailed descriptions of drug trade perils to painful shards of memory to pitch black gallows humor.
Comparing himself to one of the greatest two-sport athletes in American sports history felt natural and well-earned.

lines: On first glance, this is a cynical move: fodder for the molly-addled masses to grind their teeth.
Nothing is left to chance here: every line sticks, every beat fits like a glove.
Best of all is "Dip," perhaps the molly-related rap song that actually sounds like an MDMA experience: euphoric but also dark, jittery to the point of paranoia and teetering on the edge of disaster.

lines: Young rapper who talked about life on the street is older, wiser, and richer now.
It's just that it's shocking that he made an LP this good, a decade after the outside world first paid attention to drill.

“I’ve moved on, but my heart’s still in the trenches,” he says on the chorus of “Whole Hearts.” The distance of time hasn’t led to a distance in emotion, but it does strengthen the reflective nature of his lyrics.

lines: It’s long, messy, and full of complicated nuance that we don’t expect from our pop music, and that we don’t always even want.

He’s not the best rapper alive for 2022, not unless you consider mainstream popularity an important factor, but he’s still the most acrobatic mainstream rapper saying something, and it’s not even close.
This is an album with the best Ghostface verse in a decade, but you’ll have to get through the bastard child of Ice Cube and Yoyo’s "It’s a Man’s World" and Eminem’s "Kim" to get to it.

lines: Living through the fallout of a generational pandemic can feel stupid, confounding, unsatisfying and unreasonable.
It’s such straightforward artistry that it’s almost disarming; the simplest, barest of ingredients, distilled to whatever decadence makes sense right now.
You expect the flow to switch or the drums to kick, when really you should just shut up and eat your pasta.

lines: Back like he never left, astonishing considering how much has changed.
He sounds rejuvenated, spirited as ever, as he spills out absurd non-sequiturs and punctilious six-syllable rhyme patterns.
In the decade and a half that has followed, the man has sustained his prolific rap career and, thankfully, remained alive.

lines: For an artist prone to monotone, a 20-track set with no famous guest appearances flies in the face of trends and conventional wisdom.
To pinpoint this year as the one that killed his innocence is telling, but he doesn’t dwell on the circumstances of his upbringing, nor does he hold them in opposition wealthier kids his age.
“Senorita”, which served as the album’s lead single (though you could hardly tell if you were monitoring radio), is positively vicious.
